doc.title: Rudy Van Gelder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Later career, remasters and other interests
title: The RVG remaster series for Blue Note Japan
summary: Michael Cuscuna's call led to hundreds of RVG remasters, and Rudy contrasts them with CD transfers he had no part in.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: So maybe you can talk a little bit about how the RVG series got started.

So one summer, a long time ago, I got a call from Michael Cuscuna. Their Japanese arm of Blue Note wanted to re-issue all the masters. So a fellow by the name of Namikata decided to launch a series of RVG re-masters. First they agreed, the people who owned the tapes here, and that began a whole long process of which I made a couple of hundred or re-masters of their catalogue. And that sort of reawakened everything that was going on here, the music was going down, and then that started going up. I was doing small labels and all of the sudden I am faced with this gigantic order, taking all my time just mastering. And it was great because I was working just with the equipment here, nobody in the studio, just me and what I needed, and that was my job for a couple of years. It was just great, and it applied to some Blue Note catalogue too. And even…
Prestige, right. They were owned by…
Concord, exactly. So, that was really a nice cycle. I enjoyed that.
It was fun listening to the tapes you recorded several years ago?

Yeah. Several of them, I realized musically, hearing them for the first time, how great they were. During the session I had to be objective, you know? But when I hear the music comes back ten years later, boy, that sounded great. It gave me a second chance to hear it. The problem in what was happening is that during those early years from the 80’s on, and the C.D. those re-masters, and those transfers to digital, weren’t made by me, I had nothing to do with it. Particularly when they came out on Sony, I was not involved in any way with those masters. Everybody started to say, “Well I like the old albums better, I like the LPs” and what they were hearing was somebody’s mastering of something they had never heard, had no idea what it should sound like, just totally disregarding the fact that they should understand the music they were dealing with.
So you enjoy the opportunity to re-master those?
Oh, sure. I’d do it again.
And every time you do it you approach it…
That’s right, in a different way. I think its better that I have other equipment. I try to keep on top of things even if I don’t use them right away, I know I have it and I can use it.
